fields.description: Optimization: The radius of a theoretical bounding sphere after which the light cuts off. This is a quick cutoff but not a sharp one to prevent being confused with a bug. This further attenuates physically-correct intensity falloff. The intent is to allow tight bounds on lights that otherwise would cover a great area with minimal contribution. In general a light should be authored with this at zero (default value) or a very large number so it does not influence the physically-correct falloff, then radius should be walked back to the smallest value where no difference is practically noticed. See Cutoff Dist, which is a hard end-of-influence bound that by-design causes lighting to stop with no graceful falloff. If Attenuation Radius is larger than Cutoff Dist, this continuity will become evident.

This brush will paint a ramp between the starting point and ending point on the
given target.  A ramp is simply an interpolation of the values from the start to
the end.  To paint a ramp, click a location on the terrain and drag the mouse;
the ramp will be previewed.  Release the mouse to actually paint the ramp.
When painting a ramp on a heightfield, the result is that the height will change
from the starting point linearly to the ending point.  When painting a ramp on a
splatmask, the result is a gradient from the starting color to the ending color.
The brush parameter Amount indicates how much the ramp will be applied; it
basically represents the interpolation from the target's original value to the
ramp value.

The terrain editor supports limited Houdini integration.  To use the Houdini
integration, the proper version of Houdini must be installed.  The tools will
indicate if Houdini is not installed or not installed at the proper version.
Houdini integration works by sending the heightfield, splatmask, and selection
mask to a user-created HDA file.  The heightfield, splatmask, and selection
mask are sent to specifically-named inputs.  Likewise, the heightfield and
splatmask are output on specifically-named outputs.  User-created HDA files
must live in the Terrain Houdini folder under the project's asset branch
(tool/Terrain/Houdini).
Several user-created HDA parameters will show up in Orbit in a property panel.
Users can add integers, floating-point numbers, colors, strings, and vectors
(of length 2, 3, and 4) as parameters, and these parameters will show up in
Orbit.
Because Houdini plugins are treated like a black box, they can be difficult to
debug.  To facilitate debugging, after a plugin has been run, the user can click
the save icon to save a .HIP file that can be loaded in Houdini.  The .HIP file
is saved to the absolute path specified in the text input.

The TerrainDef asset type contains all the data needed to render the terrain.
There are several referenced assets: HeightField,
HeightField Paint, SplatMask, SplatMask Paint, Vista
Map, and Material. Both the HeightField and SplatMask have two
textures. The primary HeightField and SplatMask textures are
what will be rendered in-game as the terrain.  The other two textures (ending
in Paint) are used by the editor only for painting on the terrain. The
paint textures are 2D texture arrays, where the texture specified by <i>Source
Path will contain all the user-painted data, and the other textures are all
images that can be created by a DCC tool and act as a base layer for all
subsequent painting.
The Vista Map is a texture that represents the color of distant terrain.
The Material is the material (and materialgraph) that will be used to
render the terrain.  Terrain material graphs must expose five sub-graphs for
the splatmask layers: Base, Red, Green, Blue, and
Alpha. The textures used by these sub graphs will be overridden by the
values contained in the material paint layers.  Terrain material graphs must
also be sure to use the UVs provided by the Terrain Data not as well as
funnel the displacement to the final combiner.
The TerrainDef also allows the user to specifiy the Height of the
terrain (in meters); the Height value correlates to a value of 1 in the
grayscale heightfield texture.
Materials can be applied to the terrain by assigning material assets to the
appropriate material layer in the Terrain Def.  Note that each layer corresponds
to a specific sub-graph node (like basic_normal_gloss.materialgraph. The
textures (and overrides) specified in the material layer will be applied to the
appropriate sub graph node.  Material layers can also specify the tile size (in
meters) that the layer will be tiled across the terrain.

This is the heightfield texture asset that will be used with this piece of terrain.  It should be a 16-bit single-channel texture representing the height.  Note that the height will range from 0.0 to 1.0, and the terrain instance's matrix will take care of putting that in world space.

This is the texture asset that will be used for heightfield painting.  This is a texture array where the first layer (the 'Source File' field) is the painted data and the subsequent (optional) layers contains heightfields created by a DCC tool.  For heightfields created by DCC tools, the height should range from 0.0 to 1.0.  If no DCC heighfield is specified, a heightfield with a value of 0.0 is assumed.  The paint layer should also range from 0.0 to 1.0; however, it will lower the height of the DCC-generated heightfields if the value is less than 0.5, and raise the height of the DCC-generated heightfields if the value is greater than 0.5.  Because the paint layer can raise or lower values, the vertical granularity is halved.

This is a texture array where the first layer (the 'Source File' field) is the painted data and the second (optional) layer contains a splatmask created by a DCC tool.  For splatmasks created by DCC tools, the RGBA values should range from 0.0 to 1.0.  If no DCC splatmask is specified, a splatmask with a value of (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) is assumed.  The paint layer should also range from 0.0 to 1.0; however, it will lower the height of the DCC-generated splatmasks if the value is less than 0.5, and raise the height of the DCC-generated heightfields if the value is greater than 0.5. The terrain editor supports a variety of debug modes: Gray,
HeightField, Selection Mask, Splatmask RGBA,
Splatmask R, Splatmask G, Splatmask B,
Splatmask A, and Splatmask UVs. The HeightField
display mode will render the heightfield on the terrain instead of the
normal terrain materials. Likewise, the various SplatMask modes will
render the splatmask (or individual splatmask channels) onto the terrain instead
of the normal terrain materials. The SplatMask UVs mode will render
arrows in the direction of the positive u- and v-axes.  The
Selection Mask will render a translucent Insomniac blue over the areas
that are selected.  Note that the selection mask will render if the selection
mask is the target even if this mode isn't selected.
There are also a few ways to view the terrain wireframe. <i>Show
LoD will render the various levels of detail of the terrain in different
colors.  This helps indicate which sections of the terrain are rendering at
highter vertex counts. The Show Tiles option will render the wireframe
for each tile in a different color, making it easier to distinguish where
invidiually-rendered terrain tiles are.
The heightfield can be enabled or disabled using the Apply HeightField
deug option. The Lock Radius Axes button, when checked, will make the
brushes use a single value for the brush radius.  When unchecked, the various
axis sizes can be specified individually.
The Show Debug Grid option will enable or disable a debug grid that
renders on top of the terrain.

To create a new piece of terrain, simply open the Asset Wizard, select
Terrain, then fill out the options. Note that while a terrain instance can
be scaled in the Level Editor, the Height field represents the default height
for placed instances.  Viewing a piece of terrain in the Asset Editor will also
use this height.
Creating a piece of terrain will create 9 assets.  Assuming the new terrain is
called my_terrain, the following assets will be created:
my_terrain.terrain
This is the actual terrain asset.  A terrain asset is basically just a
container asset that points to a texture for the heightfield, a texture for the
splatmask, and a material.  It also contains a few extra textures that are only
used when painting in the editor.
my_terrain_heightfield.png
my_terrain_heightfield.texture
This is the heightfield that will be rendered in the game.  This a simple 2D
texture that has a 16-bit grayscale .png file for the source path.  This should
not be edited outside the terrain editor.
my_terrain_heightfield_paint.png
my_terrain_heightfield_paint.texture
This is the heightfield that can be painted in the tool.  This is a 2D texture
array.  Each image in the array should be a 16-bit grayscale .png.  The .png
specified by the source path in the texture is the user-painted layer of the
heightfield (there is only one).  The remaining images in the array are images
that can be generated by DCC tools.  These images should also all be 16-bit
grayscale .png files.  The DCC-generated images and the paint layer are summed
up to form the final composite layer (along with any procedurally-generated
things like roads).
my_terrain_splatmask.png
my_terrain_splatmask.texture
This is the splatmask that will be rendered in the game.  This is a simple 2D
texture that has an 8-bit RGBA .png file for the source path.  This should not
be edited outside the terrain editor.
my_terrain_splatmask_paint.png
my_terrain_splatmask_paint.texture
This is the splatmask that can be paintd by the tool.  This is a 2D texture
array.  Each image in the a rray should be an 8-bit RGBA .png.  The .png
specified by the source path in the texture is the user-painted layer of the
splatmask (there is only one).  The remaining images in the array are images
that can be generated by DCC tools.  These images should laso be 8-bit RGBA
.png files.  The DCC-generated images and the paint layer are summed up to form
the final composite layer (along with any procedurally-generated things like
roads).

Optimization: The radius of a theoretical bounding sphere after which the light cuts off. This is a quick cutoff but not a sharp one to prevent being confused with a bug. This further attenuates physically-correct intensity falloff. The intent is to allow tight bounds on lights that otherwise would cover a great area with minimal contribution. In general a light should be authored with this at zero (default value) or a very large number so it does not influence the physically-correct falloff, then radius should be walked back to the smallest value where no difference is practically noticed. See Cutoff Dist, which is a hard end-of-influence bound that by-design causes lighting to stop with no graceful falloff. If Attenuation Radius is larger than Cutoff Dist, this continuity will become evident.

fields.description:
No Shadows: The light casts no shadows, no geometry will occlude this light.
Cache Static Models: Default behavior. When the light isn't animating, all static casters are cached for performance.
Only Static Models: Cheap option for placed lights. Static models will cast shadows but dynamic ones won't. On most frames no work needs to be done to render the shadow map.
Only Dynamic Models: Useful for optimizing cinematic lighting when you only care about the shadows from the actors in the shot.
fields.name: Shadow Cast Type

fields.description:
Optimization: Higher resolutions gain detail, however have a higher fill-rate performance cost. Regardless of the setting, shadow res reduces further into the distance. If this setting is insufficient, check the following:
Scene Light Count If there are more shadowing lights than memory can bear, all shadows will be downres'ed until all fit.
Light Angle A shadow map must cover the entirety of the lit area, so wide angles on spot lights, or point lights that affect a great area will see their effective shadow resolution decrease as it's spread thinner over a greater area.
Note: Point lights actually generate 6 shadow maps, one for each cardinal axis direction/face of a cube, so they are 6x the cost of a spot light in terms of shadow cost.

Non-PBR aesthetic tweak This is intended to allow for fine control of spec response, especially in cinematics. This is an attenuation on top of the specular result, e.g. 1 is identity/do nothing, 0 means no specular, and 2 would mean twice as much specular response as is physically correct.
Non-PBR aesthetic tweak Allow light to contributed only diffuse, only specular. Normally lights should contribute both.

The bulb's shape is pushed forward along the light direction by this many meters. The purpose is to allow the light to be recessed into the ceiling/wall so that its cone is roughly the size of the bulb when it emerges. Then this push forward attribute allows the bulb to appear where it's meant to be, not at the recessed location.

fields.description:
Normally light emanates from a single point however it can be useful to ignore the micro-occlusions of light fixture geometry.
To support this, the cut on distance defines when lighting starts. The volume between the light's origin and this dead zone has no lighting. e.g. for a spot light, this would truncate the cone's tip. The transition between not-lit and lit is sharp and abrupt - there is no graceful fade-in.

fields.description: The terrain editor supports two types of brushes: bitmap brushes and HLSL
brushes.  To create a new brush, simply add it to the brush folder in the
project's asset branch (tool/Terrain/Brushes).
Bitmap Brushes
The bitmap brush is the simplest brush.  It is a grayscale image that lives in
the brush folder.  While not required, Brushes should be 16-bit to paint
heightfields with higher precision.  Brush values should range from black
to white and represent the strength with which the terrain should be painted.
HLSL Brushes
An HLSL brush is a brush that uses HLSL code to determine the strength with
which the terrain should be painted. An HLSL brush is a file with the .h
extension.  It is a text file that contains a single function that returns
a single value indicating the brush strength.  Several parameters are passed
into that function from the Terrain Editor, including a user-specified float4.
HLSL brushes show up with the HLSL tag in the brush dropdown. By
default, HLSL brushes show the brush name.  To create a custom thumbnail for
the HLSL brush, simply add a bitmap to the brushes folder with the same name
as the HLSL brush but give it the .h.thumbnail extensions.
The clipboard brush is a special brush that contains both heightfield and
splatmask information.  This brush shows up in color (showing the splatmask)
and has the Clipboard tag in the brush dropdown. The data used for
painting with this brush differs depending on if the target is the heightfield,
the splatmask, or the terrain itself.
Inverted Painting
Normally, pressing the right mouse button will increase the terrain height or
add a color to a splatmask.  However, there are times when height or color
should be removed.  There are two ways to do this.  The first way is to hold
the Shift key while painting; doing this will cause either height to be
removed from the heightfield or a color to be removed from the splatmask.  An
alternative method is to paint by pressing the left mouse button; this too will
remove height from the heightfield and color from the splatmask.  Some modes
(like Ramp) don't have an inverted mode; they will paint the same
regardless of Shift or right mouse button state. Note that holding
Shift then painting with the right-click button will not
invert the paint (think of this as a double negative, which makes a positive).
